analysis.one_liner: Strips government officials of qualified immunity so they can be sued for violating constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing or vote since it was introduced on May 23, 2025, with 18 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: When a police officer or other government official violates someone's constitutional rights, that person can sue under a Civil War-era law (Section 1983). But the Supreme Court created a protection called "qualified immunity": officials generally escape paying damages unless a prior court case had already ruled the same conduct unconstitutional. This bill would rewrite the law so that good faith, honest belief, or the absence of a clearly established rule could not be used as a defense. Victims of police misconduct and other rights violations could recover damages far more easily.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by police officers or other state and local officials. Today, qualified immunity blocks most damages claims unless the victim's lawyer can point to a prior court case ruling nearly identical conduct unconstitutional. This bill would let juries decide the facts and hold violators financially liable, and it would apply to lawsuits already in court when the bill became law. Civil-rights organizations have argued for years that this is the main obstacle to accountability for police misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of police and official misconduct

how_it_helps.text: Restores a person's ability to win money damages when a government official violates their constitutional rights, even if no court had previously ruled on that exact situation.
Makes clear that a defendant cannot escape a lawsuit by claiming they believed their conduct was lawful or acted in good faith.
Creates a deterrent: officials who know they can be held personally liable are less likely to violate constitutional rights in the first place.

analysis.who_pays: Police officers, other government officials, and the state and local governments that indemnify them. Since cities and counties typically pay judgments and settlements on their employees' behalf, the direct financial cost would largely fall on municipal budgets and their insurers — in practice, local taxpayers. Supporters respond that the change is meant to deter violations before they happen.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes every version of the good-faith defense at once, including for officials who acted when the law was genuinely unclear — opponents argue this could expose officers, teachers, and other public employees to personal liability for split-second decisions.

The change would apply to lawsuits already pending at enactment, not just future cases [S2], and because local governments routinely indemnify their employees, the cost of larger settlements would largely fall on municipal budgets and their insurers — meaning taxpayers in cities and counties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is meaningful: people whose constitutional rights are violated by government officials would regain a realistic path to compensation, and officials would face the same accountability a private citizen would. The costs are real too: officers making fast, high-stakes decisions could face liability even when the law was unsettled, and because local governments typically indemnify their employees, the money would largely come from municipal budgets and insurers — that is, taxpayers. The strongest good-faith objection is that the bill eliminates any good-faith or notice defense entirely, rather than narrowing it, which courts and police groups have argued deters people from serving in difficult public-safety jobs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has not scheduled a hearing or a vote, so it is still sitting there.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 23, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee, where any hearing, amendment, or vote would have to happen first.
The full action history shows no further action after the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.
All 19 supporters are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, which in a Republican-controlled chamber makes floor action essentially out of reach.
This is the latest in a series of identical bills Democrats have introduced in recent Congresses; none has received a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government officials and the state and local governments that insure them, who for now remain shielded by qualified immunity from being sued for constitutional violations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Shielded officials and governments that pay their claims

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 18 signed on, with no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Chairs the committee the bill was referred to; no hearing or markup has been scheduled, leaving the bill without a path to a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 supporters are Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored; Republicans hold 223 of 435 House seats, so the bill cannot move without the majority's cooperation.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and other government officials
industries.note: The bill removes the legal shield that has protected officers and other officials from personal money damages when they violate constitutional rights, even in cases where courts have found serious misconduct. It would apply to state and local officials acting under color of law.

industries.industry: Municipal governments and their liability insurers
industries.note: Cities and counties typically pay judgments and settlements on behalf of their employees, so removing qualified immunity would raise payouts in civil-rights cases and their insurance costs. Those costs ultimately pass to local taxpayers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing scheduled and no Republican support. Identical measures in recent Congresses also died in committee without a vote. Unless the committee schedules action or the political climate shifts, the bill will likely expire at the end of this Congress without a floor vote.
